summary:
Radar snapshot, 7 Oct 2026, 06:00 UTC. Plague is the only focus. Wikipedia's 'Plague (disease)' page is at 32,054 views a day, new in the top 1000. More than 70 mainstream stories ran in 72 hours, including AP, Reuters, CNN, NBC, BBC, The Guardian, The Atlantic, WSJ and Axios. The news itself is at its peak. The opening for us is to explain the questions people are typing, and to give a dated status that keeps up as facts change.

Key verified facts, as of 7 Oct 2026:
- Russian authorities say the Irkutsk worker died of 'pneumonia of undetermined origin'. They say no microorganisms linked to her work were found, and they told WHO there are no plague cases in Irkutsk.
- About 200 contacts were placed under medical observation. Per NBC, citing Russian officials, about 60% had been tested by 6 Oct. Those tests found 2 COVID-19 and 2 rhinovirus cases, and no other pathogens.
- WHO's initial risk assessment rates the risk moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for the WHO European region. Separately, WHO said that, based on unofficial information, the risk to the general population appears low.
- WHO is still asking which pathogen caused the pneumonia. It is also asking about unverified reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.
- CDC says there is 'no indication of a broader threat to the United States.'
- The story is now heavily political: Trump plans a call with Putin, Rubio and the State Department are pressing for information, and the US do-not-travel advisory for Russia has been renewed (as The Hill reported it). Unverified claims are spreading online, and France 24 has fact-checked them.

The calm, attributed decoder is our best opening because it is our most repeatable formula. Much of the coverage leans on politics or fear ('should scare you', 'we should be terrified'). Note that 'suspected plague' has shifted to 'Russia says not plague, WHO wants the pathogen'. Every status piece must carry that shift and a date.

Evergreen Plague 101 searches have huge demand right now: is it contagious, symptoms, is it curable, US cases, pneumonic vs bubonic. They will keep pulling traffic after the news fades.

What to avoid:
- Anything that speculates about a bioweapon, a cover-up or the person who died.
- Any topic that drifts into politics.

candidates.topic: Irkutsk 'plague' case status decoder: Russia says no plague found, WHO still waiting on the pathogen (as of Oct 7, 2026)
candidates.angle:
Confirmed vs reported vs unknown, in 3 columns, each dated and attributed:
- Russia: pneumonia of undetermined origin, no plague, contact tests found 2 COVID and 2 rhinovirus cases.
- WHO: risk rated moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia, very low for Europe; still asking for the pathogen.
- CDC: no indication of a broader US threat.
We lay out the facts calmly and add no speculation. Re-check every source at publish time.
candidates.why_now: The official status flipped within 48 hours, from 'suspected pneumonic plague' to 'Russia says no plague'. Many viewers still believe it is confirmed plague. Each new statement (from WHO, Rospotrebnadzor or after the Trump–Putin call) gives us a fresh 'as of [date]' hook. Decoders are our best-proven format (3 for 3).

evidence.signal: Russia says no plague found in contacts. About 60% of contacts tested, with 2 COVID and 2 rhinovirus cases. CDC: no indication of a broader US threat.
Russia tells WHO there are no plague cases in the Siberian city
How Russia and the world are responding. Covers WHO's risk statements.
Plague (disease) page at 32,054 views a day, new in the top 1000

candidates.topic: Can pneumonic plague spread person to person? Close-contact respiratory droplets, not long-range airborne spread like measles
candidates.angle: Answer within 10 seconds: yes, but mainly through close, face-to-face contact with someone who is coughing and already sick. That is why contact tracing a defined group, like the ~200 people in Irkutsk, works. Name both comparators: measles and COVID. Close on what stops it: early antibiotics for contacts. Include the 'talk to a health professional' line.
keywords: can plague spread person to person
candidates.why_now: Contagion is the top question in every explainer headline (NBC, CBS, CNN, Sacramento Bee, PBS). Search intent is strong and an evergreen-style answer works whatever the final diagnosis turns out to be. It is the playbook's search-question formula.

evidence.signal: What is pneumonic plague and how dangerous is it?
A microbiologist explains the case and pneumonic transmission
What is pneumonic plague, and how will we know if it's spreading?

candidates.topic: Is plague curable? Antibiotics work well when started early, and why timing matters most for pneumonic plague
candidates.angle: A calm, honest answer. Plague is treatable with common antibiotics. Untreated pneumonic plague is very often fatal, and fast treatment changes that. Contacts can be given preventive antibiotics by health authorities. Name no specific drug doses and give no stockpiling advice. Use the urgent-care line.
candidates.why_now: Fear-driven 'is there a cure' searches follow every plague headline. Online myths say 'no cure'. Our 'not proven / here's what stops it' style of honesty did best in our data (113 views).

evidence.signal: What to know about plague amid reports of the lab worker's death
What to know about a suspected death from pneumonic plague

candidates.topic: Plague in the US: about 7 human cases a year (CDC), mostly bubonic, mostly in the rural West
candidates.angle:
Put the US-local fact first:
- An average of 7 cases a year (range 0–17).
- Most are in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada.
- Over 80% are bubonic.
Then practical, CDC-based prevention: flea control on pets, avoid handling sick or dead rodents, and see a doctor promptly with fever after possible exposure.
keywords: how many plague cases a year us
candidates.why_now: The Hill and NEWS10 are running 'Plague cases still occur in the US: here's where'. US viewers are asking 'could it happen here?' This is a concrete, verifiable number plus practical steps, the playbook's number+fix formula.

evidence.signal: Average of 7 US human cases a year (range 0–17); over 80% bubonic
Plague cases still occur in the US: here's where

candidates.topic: Pneumonic vs bubonic vs septicemic plague: the 3 forms of Yersinia pestis infection and why only pneumonic passes person to person
candidates.angle: A named three-way comparison: how each starts (flea bite, the bloodstream, the lungs), typical signs and how each spreads. The punchline: pneumonic plague is the rare form, and the only one that spreads between people through coughing.
candidates.why_now: Search volume for 'what is pneumonic plague' spiked with the story (Sacramento Bee, PBS, WOWK and Hindustan Times explainers). It is a durable search asset for long-form and carousels.

evidence.signal: Understanding pneumonic plague after the lab worker's death
Plague (disease) page at 32k views a day

candidates.topic: How ~200 contacts are monitored: contact tracing, observation, preventive antibiotics and isolation after a suspected pneumonic plague exposure
candidates.angle: A dated official number plus how it works. The figure: about 200 contacts placed under medical observation; per NBC, citing Russian officials, about 60% had been tested by 6 Oct. Then the public-health playbook, step by step: identify contacts, monitor through the incubation window, give preventive antibiotics if a clinician advises it, isolate anyone who gets symptoms. Use Madagascar 2017 as the large-scale example.
candidates.why_now: '200 under observation' is the most repeated number in the coverage (New Scientist, National News Desk, Reuters). Few creators explain the mechanism. This matches our number+fix formula (needle-sticks, 46).

evidence.signal: Nearly 200 people isolated after the lab worker's death
About 60% of contacts tested; no plague found, per Russian officials
Institute staff isolated after the worker's death

candidates.topic: WHO's risk rating for the Irkutsk case, decoded: moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia, very low for Europe
candidates.angle: An attributed correction for viewers who saw 'pandemic' headlines: what WHO actually said, what each risk tier means, and what would change the rating (confirmation of the pathogen, new linked cases). Date-stamped. CDC's US statement sits alongside.
candidates.why_now: Al Jazeera, RFE/RL, CNBC, Katie Couric Media and Vox all frame the question as 'should we be worried?'. Our answer is named-agency wording, our attributed-correction formula (44).

evidence.signal: WHO says plague epidemic risk in Russia is low
Global risk maybe low, but experts want more data
CDC is monitoring and 'prepared'

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague symptoms and incubation: what the first days look like, and when to seek urgent care
candidates.angle: Symptoms in timeline order: sudden fever, headache, weakness, then rapidly worsening pneumonia with cough and chest pain. Use the incubation window from CDC and WHO. Note that early symptoms look like flu, which is also what Russia said about how this case first presented. Make the urgent-care line explicit: contact a doctor or local health authority right away if you have possible exposure plus symptoms. Do not encourage self-diagnosis.
candidates.why_now: WHO reported that the case 'initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection', which makes 'plague vs flu' a natural question. Flu season is starting, which adds anxiety about symptoms.

evidence.signal: Pneumonic plague: what it is and how dangerous it can be
WHO: the illness initially presented as an acute respiratory viral infection

candidates.topic: How high-containment labs that study plague keep it contained (BSL-3), and what happens after a possible lab exposure
candidates.angle:
Lab safety explained with no speculation about this incident:
- What BSL-3 means: airflow, protective gear, sealed cabinets, medical surveillance.
- What happens after a possible exposure: reporting, observation, preventive antibiotics.
- Anti-plague institutes routinely study natural plague foci.
Use only details reported by named sources.
candidates.why_now: This is the third snapshot this topic has appeared in, holding at 72/70. CNN ('checklists, masks and mystery') and the Atlantic Council are covering the lab angle. Few health creators explain biosafety calmly, so the bar is low.

evidence.signal: Checklists, masks and mystery: what we know about the plague scare
Five things to know about the death at Russia's anti-plague laboratory

candidates.topic: 'Second case' reports: WHO is asking about an unverified second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause (as of Oct 7)
candidates.angle: A rumour-vs-record Short. Russian outlets reported a second case. WHO's Director-General said WHO has sought details. Nothing is officially confirmed yet. Explain why 'reported' is not 'confirmed', and update as soon as WHO or Russian authorities answer.
keywords: is there a second plague case
candidates.why_now: Forbes and UNITED24 surfaced this overnight. Search spikes when an official answer arrives. We should be ready with a factual template and must not run the claim before it is verified.

evidence.signal: WHO seeks details about a reported second illness
Russian media report a second death (unverified)

candidates.topic: Plague myths corrected: 'no cure', 'airborne like COVID', 'it's the Black Death again'
candidates.angle: Fact-check the 3 most-shared plague beliefs, each corrected by a named agency (WHO, CDC). France 24 has documented unverified claims spreading. We correct the health myths only and never repeat the bioweapon or cover-up framing.
keywords: is there a cure for plague
candidates.why_now: France 24's 'Truth or Fake' segment and ABC Australia report rumours spreading online. Myth-busts work best when they target a belief viewers already hold.

evidence.signal: Unverified claims about the lab worker's death spread online
Russia rails against online 'plague' claims

candidates.topic: Black Death (1347) vs 2026: what antibiotics, germ theory and contact tracing changed
candidates.angle: A comparison that names both sides: what killed so many people in the 1300s (no knowledge of germs or fleas, no antibiotics) vs what we have now (diagnosis, antibiotics, preventive treatment, surveillance). We use history to reassure, with no doom imagery.
keywords: could the black death happen again
candidates.predicted_peak: ongoing; boost over the next 7 days
candidates.why_now: Every Black Death video sees a surge in views when plague is in the news. The Hill links the scare to pandemic memories. A reassuring explanation of what has changed is the opposite of the fear framing most creators use.

evidence.signal: Plague in Russia sparks concern and COVID pandemic memories: 5 things to know
Plague is back in the news (history explainer)

candidates.topic: Madagascar 2017: how a large pneumonic plague outbreak was stopped with contact tracing and preventive antibiotics
candidates.angle: A real-world case study showing that outbreaks of the pneumonic form can be controlled. Cover what WHO and Madagascar did (tracing, preventive antibiotics for contacts, treatment centres) and the outcome. All figures come from WHO's situation reports.
candidates.why_now: Viewers are asking 'how will we know if it's spreading?' (Washington Post). A concrete precedent answers 'what stops it' calmly. Almost no creators cover it.

evidence.signal: How will we know if it's spreading in Russia?
Global response explainer

candidates.topic: Plague, pets and fleas: how cats and dogs can bring plague home in the US West, and CDC prevention steps
candidates.angle: Practical and local. Cats are especially susceptible and can pass plague on. Cover flea control and keeping pets away from rodent burrows, and tell owners to see a vet if a pet in a plague area gets sick. Everything is CDC-sourced and calm.
candidates.why_now: The 'US cases' coverage is pushing readers toward prevention. Many US human cases involve pets or wildlife. Competition is low and the topic is safe and useful.

evidence.signal: US cases are concentrated in the rural West
Plague cases still occur in the US: here's where

candidates.topic: Is there a plague vaccine? Status as of Oct 2026
candidates.angle: An honest 'not available for the public' answer. There is no widely licensed plague vaccine for general use in the US or UK. Early antibiotics and prevention are the tools. Mention research candidates only with their trial stage, and date-hedge everything.
keywords: is there a vaccine for plague
candidates.why_now: 'Vaccine' is a natural follow-up search once people learn plague is treatable. Competition is low. Vaccine status is listed in the treatment pillar.

evidence.signal: Covers how dangerous pneumonic plague is and how it is treated

candidates.topic: US–Russia politics around the case: the Trump–Putin call, Rubio's demands and the US travel advisory
candidates.angle: Not recommended as a standalone piece. It is political, and it invites cover-up and bioweapon speculation that our guardrails forbid. Use only as a one-line dated status fact inside the decoder (e.g. 'CDC: no indication of a broader US threat').
candidates.why_now: Heavy political coverage (CNBC, NBC, FT, Washington Post, BBC), but it falls outside the health mission and risks stigmatising a country.

evidence.signal: Trump has a call scheduled with Putin about the possible pneumonic plague case
